newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS - WMC sees 1st half profit drop.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS - WMC sees 1st half profit drop.

text.p: Australian base metals and gold group WMC Ltd on Friday warned softening world metal prices and a rising Australian dollar would substantially reduce profits in the first half of 1996/97 and beyond if they persisted.

Chairman Sir Arvi Parbo told WMC's annual meeting that while costs were being cut, a continued higher exchange rate and lower prices for WMC's key commodities -- nickel, copper and aluminium -- would adversely affect the full year result.
WMC's moves to cut costs would counter some of the negative effects of lower prices and the higher exchange rate.
"But it is obvious that should the lower prices and the higher exchange rate persist for the rest of the current financial year, the financial result for 1996/97 will be affected adversely," he said.
"The profit for the first half will be substantially lower than for the first half of last year," he said, adding it was difficult to judge how long these conditions would persist.
There were some indications the downturn may have bottomed and some observers were predicting an improvement in the demand for metals and minerals in 1997, he said.
"Time will tell whether they are right," he said.
WMC earned a net A$386.2 million in the 1995/96 year ended June 30 after earning A$186.2 million in the first half.

With the company expecting to sell off its petroleum assets by June 1997, Parbo unveiled plans to consolidate WMC's Australian gold operations and indicated final approval could be expected soon for a long-awaited phosphate project.

The board had approved a A$157 million gold processing plant at St Ives, Western Australia, with construction to begin early next year, to treat initially five million tonnes of ore and ultimately seven million tonnes a year, he said.
When completed in 1998, it expected St Ives' gold production to rise to around 550,000 ounces a year and subsequently 700,000 ounces, up from the current level of around 400,000 ounces.
St Ives has produced three million ounces of gold since 1981 with reserves and resources are currently 6.7 million ounces.

Parbo said with the concentration on the St Ives potential, WMC had decided to offer for sale by tender in the first quarter of 1997 its Hill 50 gold operation at Mt Magnet, where production fell 23.7 percent to 133,000 ounces in 1995/96.
WMC also said it was nearing final approval for the long mooted development of its major phosphate resource near Mt Isa in Queensland into a high analysis fertiliser project.

Managing director Hugh Morgan said the proposed A$650 million project could be operational by the turn of the century and would not require a further share issue but could be funded from existing cashflow and borrowings.
"This is one of the world's great phosphate deposits, containing over two billion tonnes of resources with low impurities," he told shareholders.

Detailing the outlook for its key commodity groups, Morgan said WMC was targeting a ten percent cut in nickel unit costs by the end of 1996/97, through increased efficiencies and improved work practices.

He said the recent decline in nickel prices reflected a reduction in demand from the stainless steel industry, but the outlook for stainless steel consumption was, however, good and hence nickel demand remained positive in the longer term.
Evidence pointed to some strengthening of alumina prices from the low point of mid-1996 and WMC expected stronger demand for aluminium and alumina as economic conditions improved.

Morgan was buoyant about prospects for selling additional uranium to be produced in WMC's A$1.25 billion expansion of its Olympic Dam copper-uranium mine in South Australia, saying it faced "very enthusiastic demand" from international utilities.
With Olympic Dam's copper production to double to 200,000 tonnes, he said demand for copper was expected to grow steadily at about three percent a year over the long term.
He said WMC was hardened to the fact that commodity prices rose and fell. However, costs were also coming down and so he saw the opportunities to build the business as substantial.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
